fetched_contents.text: Prebiotic galactooligosaccharide improves piglet growth performance and intestinal health associated with alterations of the hindgut microbiota during the peri-weaning period Abstract Background Weaning stress reduces growth performance and health of young pigs due in part to an abrupt change in diets from highly digestible milk to fibrous plant-based feedstuffs. This study investigated whether dietary galactooligosaccharide (GOS), supplemented both pre- and post-weaning, could improve growth performance and intestinal health via alterations in the hindgut microbial community. Methods Using a 3 × 2 factorial design, during farrowing 288 piglets from 24 litters received either no creep feed (FC), creep without GOS (FG–) or creep with 5% GOS (FG+) followed by a phase 1 nursery diet without (NG–) or with 3.8% GOS (NG+). Pigs were sampled pre- (D22) and post-weaning (D31) to assess intestinal measures. Results Creep fed pigs grew 19% faster than controls (P < 0.01) prior to weaning, and by the end of the nursery phase (D58), pigs fed GOS pre-farrowing (FG+) were 1.85 kg heavier than controls (P < 0.05). Furthermore, pigs fed GOS in phase 1 of the nursery grew 34% faster (P < 0.04), with greater feed intake and efficiency. Cecal microbial communities clustered distinctly in pre- vs. post-weaned pigs, based on principal coordinate analysis (P < 0.01). No effects of GOS were detected pre-weaning, but gruel creep feeding increased Chao1 α-diversity and altered several genera in the cecal microbiota (P < 0.05). Post-weaning, GOS supplementation increased some genera such as Fusicatenibacter and Collinsella, whereas others decreased such as Campylobacter and Frisingicoccus (P < 0.05). Changes were accompanied by higher molar proportions of butyrate in the cecum of GOS-fed pigs (P < 0.05). Conclusions Gruel creep feeding effectively improves suckling pig growth regardless of GOS treatment. When supplemented post-weaning, prebiotic GOS improves piglet growth performance associated with changes in hindgut microbial composition. Keywords: Galactooligosaccharide, Gut microbiome, Intestinal villi, Prebiotics, Weaning Background The nursery period in swine production is challenged with high rates of morbidity and mortality stemming from stark reductions in feed intake owing to abrupt changes in diet composition, socio-hierarchical challenges, and overall weaning stress. Dietary antibiotics have historically been utilized post-weaning due to their ability to decrease pathogenic bacteria. However, there are growing concerns of antimicrobial resistant bacteria due to the excess use of antibiotics in swine feeds [1]. To mitigate the negative impacts of weaning and shift away from antibiotics, the use of creep feeding during farrowing and the supplementation of prebiotics during the farrowing and nursery periods have been explored as potential solutions. Supplementing sow’s milk with creep feed to suckling piglets is a practice that has been employed for many years and has several benefits such as increased weaning weight, feed familiarity, and post-weaning feed intake [2–4]. Whereas some studies report that intake of dry creep feed may be negligible [5], there are several innovations such as liquid gruel creep diets that increase intakes of creep feed [6, 7]. Prebiotics are nondigestible feed ingredients that promote the growth of beneficial microorganisms in the gut. Different prebiotics range from mannan-oligosaccharides, fructo-oligosaccharides, to galactooligosaccharides (GOS). They are commonly introduced as a supplement to swine nursery diets where their fermentation may increase short chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, shift microbial communities and impact immunologic and metabolic processes in the GI tract [8–11]. Whereas prebiotics were originally seen as a replacement of cellulose for a more digestible fiber source [12], we now have sequencing technologies to examine detailed gut microbial changes induced by prebiotic inclusion in diets [13]. Given that galactose is a natural constituent of milk, GOS may be particularly well-suited for use in early life. Indeed, commercial GOS products are generally recognized as safe and have been used as prebiotics in formulas for infants [14]. GOS is synthesized by incubating high concentrations of lactose with beta-galactosidase. Under such conditions, lactose is hydrolyzed and the resulting galactose is polymerized via β-glycosidic bonds, yielding adducts containing 2–20 monomers [15]. In suckling pigs, [16, 17] GOS feeding was associated with altered intestinal microbiota composition, increased SCFA concentrations and tended to improve histomorphology. When fed to weanling pigs, GOS also increased fiber fermentation and SCFA concentrations accompanied by changes in microbial composition [18, 19]. Predicated on this previous research, the aim of the current experiment was to determine if supplementing prebiotic GOS to pigs both pre- and post-weaning would stimulate fermentation and facilitate weaning transition. Accordingly, our hypothesis was that GOS feeding would improve piglet growth performance by altering several parameters including intestinal morphology, SCFA concentrations, microbial composition and plasma cytokines. fetched_contents.text: Dietary supplementation with soybean oligosaccharides increases short-chain fatty acids but decreases protein-derived catabolites in the intestinal luminal content of weaned Huanjiang mini-piglets Abstract The improvement of gut health and function with prebiotic supplements after weaning is an active area of research in pig nutrition. The present study was conducted to test the working hypothesis that medium-term dietary supplementation with soybean oligosaccharides (SBOS) can affect the gut ecosystem in terms of microbiota composition, luminal bacterial short-chain fatty acid and ammonia concentrations, and intestinal expression of genes related to intestinal immunity and barrier function. Ten Huanjiang mini-piglets, weaned at 21 days of age, were randomly assigned to 2 groups. Each group received a standard diet containing either dietary supplementation with 0.5% corn starch (control group) or 0.5% SBOS (experimental group). The results showed that dietary supplementation with SBOS increased the diversity of intestinal microflora and elevated (P < .05) the numbers of some presumably beneficial intestinal bacteria (eg, Bifidobacterium sp, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Fusobacterium prausnitzii, and Roseburia). Soybean oligosaccharide supplementation also increased the concentration of short-chain fatty acid in the intestinal lumen, and it reduced (P < .05) the numbers of bacteria with pathogenic potential (eg, Escherichia coli, Clostridium, and Streptococcus) and the concentration of several protein-derived catabolites (eg, isobutyrate, isovalerate, and ammonia). In addition, SBOS supplementation increased (P < .05) expression of zonula occludens 1 messenger RNA, and it decreased (P < .05) expression of tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin 1β, and interleukin 8 messenger RNA in the ileum and colon. These findings suggest that SBOS supplementation modifies the intestinal ecosystem in weaned Huanjiang mini-piglets and has potentially beneficial effects on the gut. Introduction Previous reports focusing on gut microbiota and metabolism in relation to animal gastrointestinal physiology reveal a complex regulation of metabolism and physiology in the intestinal mucosa that involves bacterial compounds and metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and ammonia [1]. Increasing attention has been paid to the use of functional dietary supplements, such as prebiotics, which modulate the microbial community composition and metabolism in a presumably beneficial way [2]. This is due, even more so, to their capacity to selectively stimulate the growth and/or activities of endogenous bacteria with potentially beneficial effects (including Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium) in the colon [3]. One major aim of prebiotic supplementation during critical periods, such as pig weaning, is to avoid growth of bacterial species in the gut that could have potentially adverse effects on the host and to relieve stress-associated gut injury [4]. Soybean oligosaccharides (SBOSs) have been designated as “generally recognized as safe” material in the United States with a presumed, but not proven, “prebiotic identity.” Our previous studies indicated that SBOS can be selectively fermented by commensal bacteria in the colon, thus improving the balance of gut microflora while modulating metabolism in vitro [5]. Therefore, in view of the potential interest in SBOS as a prebiotic supplement, we developed our working hypothesis. In this study, we hypothesized that medium-term dietary supplementation with SBOS in weaned piglets can affect the gut ecosystem, both in bacterial metabolites and in microbiota composition and gene expression in the intestine. Therefore, we used the Huanjiang mini-piglet model to analyze the microbiota composition. Specifically, we examined the luminal composition of several bacterial metabolites (including bacterial SCFA and iso-SCFA) and the amount of ammonia in the distal part of the small intestine and the colon (where bacterial concentration is high). In addition, gene expression in relation to intestinal immunity (proinflammatory cytokines) and the barrier function of the epithelium (tight junction–associated proteins) were measured to determine if putative changes in the intestinal luminal content were associated with modifications of gene expression in the host. To maintain the integrity of the intestinal barrier and promote the digestion and absorption of nutrients and other physiological activities, it is beneficial if the host has a stable gut microbial community. The composition of the gut microbiota is influenced by many factors, such as genetic and environmental factors, and it changes with age. Throughout pig growth and development, the porcine gut microbiota constantly changes in composition. The NSP can be divided into insoluble NSP (mainly cellulose) and soluble NSP (composed mainly of pectic polymers, which are partially soluble in water). Monogastric animals do not have the enzymes to hydrolyze these carbohydrates, and thus their digestion occurs by means of bacterial fermentation. The fermentation of soybean carbohydrates produces short chain fatty acids that can be used as an energy source by animals. The utilization efficiency of the carbohydrates is related to the chemical structure, the level of inclusion in the diet, species and age of the animal. In poultry, soluble NSP can increase digesta viscosity, reduce the digestibility of nutrients and depress growth performance. In growing pigs, these effects, in particular the effect on gut viscosity, are often not so obvious. However, in weaning piglets, it is reported that soy oligosaccharides and soluble NSP can cause detrimental effects on intestinal health. In monogastrics, consideration must be given to the anti-nutritive effect of the NSP on nutrient digestion and absorption on one hand, as well as the potential benefits or detriments of intestinal fermentation products to the host. This mirrors the needs for i) increasing efficiency of utilization of fibrous materials in monogastrics, and ii) the maintenance and improvement of animal health in antibiotic-free production systems, on the other hand. For example, ethanol/water extraction removes the low molecular weight carbohydrate fractions, such as the oligosaccharides and part of the soluble pectins, leaving behind the insoluble fraction of the NSP, which is devoid of anti-nutritive activities. The resultant product is a high quality soy protein concentrate. This paper presents the composition and chemical structures of carbohydrates present in soybeans and discusses their nutritive and anti-nutritive effects on digestion and absorption of nutrients in pigs and poultry. Direct evidence for intestinal physiology in weaning piglets suggests that soy oligosaccharides can influence intestinal morphology, barrier markers, and physiology in a dose- and treatment-specific way, but the evidence base is mixed and not uniformly supportive.

On intestinal morphology and villus/crypt ratios, the available evidence is indirect but suggestive. A prebiotic galactooligosaccharide (GOS) study in piglets found that pre-weaning creep feeding improved growth and intestinal health, and that GOS supplementation post-weaning increased some genera such as Fusicatenibacter and Collinsella while decreasing others such as Campylobacter and Frisingicoccus [N1-F2]. The study also reported that cecal microbial communities clustered distinctly pre- versus post-weaning, and that pre-weaning GOS effects were not apparent, whereas post-weaning GOS effects were more detectable [N1-F2]. Although this is not a direct comparison of soy oligosaccharides to other oligosaccharides, it implies that oligosaccharide type and timing of supplementation can shape intestinal microbial and morphological outcomes. Additional evidence from poultry-related studies indicates that dietary soy galactooligosaccharides affect performance and that villus height, crypt depth, and their ratio are indicators of gut health [N2-R1]. Another poultry-related study reported that fermented soybean meal with mannan oligosaccharide improved gut morphology by increasing villus height and reducing crypt depth [N2-R2]. Together, these sources support the general idea that oligosaccharides can alter villus-crypt dynamics, but they do not prove a uniform effect for soy oligosaccharides in weaning piglets.

On intestinal barrier markers and permeability, the evidence is stronger in the prebiotic GOS study. The study reported that GOS supplementation increased some presumably beneficial intestinal bacteria, elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and reduced the numbers of bacteria with pathogenic potential such as Escherichia coli, Clostridium, and Streptococcus [N3-F1]. It also found increased expression of zonula occludens 1 (ZO-1) mRNA and reduced expression of proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin 1β, and interleukin 8 mRNA in the ileum and colon [N3-F1]. These findings are consistent with improved intestinal barrier function and reduced inflammation. However, the cited evidence does not explicitly quantify intestinal permeability or provide direct measurements of permeability markers such as transepithelial resistance or endotoxin translocation. So, while the evidence supports barrier-related benefits, the degree of permeability change remains only indirectly supported [N3-F1].

On dose-dependent or treatment-specific responses, the evidence is mixed. The GOS study used a 3 × 2 factorial design with 5% GOS in creep feed and 3.8% GOS in phase 1 nursery feed, and found that pre-weaning effects were not apparent, whereas post-weaning GOS effects were more detectable [N1-F2]. This suggests a treatment-specific and timing-dependent response. A separate review notes that soy oligosaccharides and soluble NSP can cause detrimental effects on intestinal health in weaning piglets [N5-F3], which is a cautionary context for dose-dependent adverse effects. Another review also notes that soluble NSP can increase digesta viscosity, reduce nutrient digestibility, and depress growth performance in poultry, with less obvious effects in growing pigs but reported detrimental effects in weaning piglets [N5-F3]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that oligosaccharide inclusion can be dose-dependent and context-specific, with potential benefits at some levels and risks at others, especially during early post-weaning transitions [N5-F3].

Overall, the direct evidence points to intestinal physiology effects that are largely treatment-specific, with some improvements in barrier markers and microbial composition, but also with evidence of possible antinutrient or digestion-related limitations in weaning piglets [N1-F2][N3-F1][N5-F3].

Direct evidence on microbial activity and fermentation outcomes in weaning piglets indicates that soy oligosaccharides can shift dominant bacterial taxa, increase SCFA production, and alter microbial fermentation patterns, but the evidence is also somewhat mixed in terms of persistence and consistency across studies.

On shifts in dominant bacterial taxa and community structure, the strongest direct evidence comes from the soybean oligosaccharide study in weaned Huanjiang mini-piglets. That study reported increased diversity of intestinal microflora and elevated numbers of presumably beneficial intestinal bacteria such as Bifidobacterium sp, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Fusobacterium prausnitzii, and Roseburia [N3-F1]. It also found reduced numbers of bacteria with pathogenic potential such as Escherichia coli, Clostridium, and Streptococcus [N3-F1]. The study also observed distinct cecal microbial community clustering pre- versus post-weaning, indicating that the microbiota is developmentally dynamic and that oligosaccharide supplementation can shift community structure [N1-F2]. In addition, a broader review notes that soy oligosaccharides and soluble NSP can cause detrimental effects on intestinal health in weaning piglets [N5-F3], which suggests that microbiota shifts can be context-dependent and not always beneficial.

On changes in SCFA production and microbial fermentation patterns, the evidence is similarly positive but not universal. The soy oligosaccharide study found increased short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the intestinal lumen and reduced protein-derived catabolites such as isobutyrate, isovalerate, and ammonia [N3-F1]. The same study also reported that SBOS supplementation increased zonula occludens 1 mRNA and reduced proinflammatory cytokine expression, supporting a broader fermentative and barrier-related benefit [N3-F1]. A separate review and evidence snippet note that fermentation of soybean carbohydrates produces short-chain fatty acids that can be used as an energy source by animals, and that dietary supplementation with soybean oligosaccharides increases SCFAs while decreasing protein-derived catabolites in the intestinal luminal content [N4-R4][N3-F1]. This reinforces the view that oligosaccharide inclusion can promote fermentative activity and alter microbial metabolism. However, the evidence does not consistently show a single dominant SCFA profile across all studies, so the fermentation effect appears to be species-specific, dose-specific, and context-specific [N3-F1][N4-R4].

On whether effects are transient or persistent after treatment, the evidence is limited but suggestive of a transient benefit. The soy oligosaccharide study was a medium-term supplementation experiment in weaned piglets, and the authors conclude that SBOS supplementation modifies the intestinal ecosystem with potentially beneficial effects on the gut [N3-F1]. The review also notes that prebiotic effects are often determined by the chemical structure, level of inclusion, species, and age of the animal, and that effects can be transient or persistent depending on these factors [N5-F3]. The GOS study in piglets found that pre-weaning effects were not detectable, whereas post-weaning effects were more apparent, suggesting that the microbiota and fermentation response may be more persistent after the transition period [N1-F2]. Still, the direct evidence does not provide long-term follow-up to establish whether the changes are sustained beyond the study period.

Overall, the direct evidence supports a pro-fermentative microbial shift with increased SCFA production and reduced pathogen-like bacterial load, but the effects are clearly context-dependent, and the literature indicates that they may not be universally persistent or uniformly beneficial in all weaning piglet studies [N3-F1][N4-R4][N5-F3].

The study design, dose response, and antinutrient/digestion context for soy oligosaccharides in weaning piglets indicate that the evidence is heterogeneous, with both supportive and cautionary findings.

On dose levels, duration, and treatment-specific study designs, the evidence shows a range of approaches. The prebiotic GOS study used a 3 × 2 factorial design, with 5% GOS in creep feed and 3.8% GOS in phase 1 nursery feed, and included both pre- and post-weaning supplementation [N1-F2]. This design is useful because it separates timing from dose, but it is specific to galactooligosaccharides rather than soy oligosaccharides. A separate soy oligosaccharide study in weaned Huanjiang mini-piglets used a medium-term supplementation period with 0.5% SBOS in the diet [N3-F1]. Another review notes that soluble NSP can increase digesta viscosity, reduce nutrient digestibility, and depress growth performance in poultry, with less obvious effects in growing pigs but reported detrimental effects in weaning piglets [N5-F3]. This suggests that study designs must account for age and dietary composition, because the same carbohydrate can behave differently across species and life stages.

On evidence for dose-response relationships, the evidence is mixed. The GOS study found that pre-weaning effects were not apparent, whereas post-weaning GOS effects were more detectable, which is consistent with a dose-response or timing-dependent response rather than a simple linear dose-response [N1-F2]. The soy oligosaccharide study in weaned piglets found that SBOS increased short-chain fatty acids and reduced protein-derived catabolites, but it was a medium-term experiment with a single dose level of 0.5% SBOS [N3-F1]. A separate review notes that prebiotic effects are related to chemical structure, level of inclusion, species, and age of the animal, and that effects can be transient or persistent depending on these factors [N5-F3]. This supports the idea that dose-response relationships are likely nonlinear and context-dependent rather than uniform.

On antinutrient or digestion-related limitations and enzyme interactions, the evidence is cautionary. The review explicitly states that soy oligosaccharides and soluble NSP can cause detrimental effects on intestinal health in weaning piglets [N5-F3]. It also explains that monogastric animals lack the enzymes to hydrolyze these carbohydrates, so digestion occurs by bacterial fermentation, which can produce SCFAs but also may have anti-nutritive effects on nutrient digestion and absorption [N5-F3]. Another source reports that supplementing α-galactosidase can improve digestibility of soybean oligosaccharides in nursery diets of newly weaned pigs [N5-R2], which suggests that enzyme supplementation is a practical response to oligosaccharide digestion limitations. A broader review also notes that soluble NSP can increase digesta viscosity, reduce nutrient digestibility, and depress growth performance, with more pronounced effects in weaning piglets [N5-F3]. This indicates that oligosaccharides can create digestion and absorption challenges that may require enzyme supplementation or careful dietary formulation.

Overall, the study design and dose-response context suggest that soy oligosaccharides can have meaningful physiological effects, but the evidence is not uniform and must be interpreted with caution. The same carbohydrate can be beneficial in some contexts and harmful in others, especially in weaning piglets, and enzyme interactions may be necessary to mitigate digestion-related limitations [N5-F3][N5-R2].

Mechanistic and contextual factors that explain the effects of soy oligosaccharides in weaning piglets include both prebiotic-like fermentation mechanisms and diet- and nutrient-specific interactions, but the evidence also highlights important limitations and gaps.

On possible prebiotic vs fermentable substrate mechanisms, the evidence supports the idea that soy oligosaccharides act as fermentable substrates rather than simply as inert fibers. The review notes that monogastric animals lack the enzymes to hydrolyze these carbohydrates, so digestion occurs by bacterial fermentation, producing SCFAs that can be used as an energy source [N5-F3]. The soy oligosaccharide study in weaned piglets explicitly found increased short-chain fatty acid concentrations and reduced protein-derived catabolites in the intestinal lumen [N3-F1]. This is consistent with a prebiotic-like mechanism in which oligosaccharides selectively stimulate beneficial microbial fermentation and reduce harmful metabolites. However, the same evidence also notes that SBOS is generally regarded as “generally recognized as safe” but not yet proven as a prebiotic, and that its effects depend on the host microbiota and the metabolic context [N3-F1]. So the evidence supports a fermentable-substrate mechanism but also emphasizes that the prebiotic identity is not yet fully established.

On dietary interactions and nutrient competition effects, the evidence is clear that oligosaccharides can compete with other nutrients and dietary components. The review states that soluble NSP can increase digesta viscosity, reduce nutrient digestibility, and depress growth performance in poultry, with less obvious effects in growing pigs but reported detrimental effects in weaning piglets [N5-F3]. It also notes that the anti-nutritive effects of NSP on nutrient digestion and absorption must be balanced against the potential benefits of fermentation products [N5-F3]. In other words, oligosaccharides can improve gut fermentation and barrier function, but they can also interfere with nutrient availability, especially when included at higher levels. The enzyme-supplementation context is especially important here: α-galactosidase can improve digestibility of soybean oligosaccharides in nursery diets [N5-R2], suggesting that dietary interactions can be mitigated with enzyme supplementation. This indicates that the effects are not purely metabolic; they depend on the overall diet composition and the presence of other fermentable or non-fermentable ingredients.

Another poultry-related study reported that fermented soybean meal with mannan oligosaccharide improved gut morphology by increasing villus height and reducing crypt depth [N2-R2]. However, the evidence is not uniform. The review notes that soy oligosaccharides and soluble non-starch polysaccharides can cause detrimental effects on intestinal health in weaning piglets [N5-F3]. This cautionary context suggests that the physiological response is treatment-specific and may depend on dose, timing, and the broader dietary environment [N1-F2][N5-F3].

### 2) Microbial activity and fermentation outcomes: shifts in taxa, SCFA production, and persistence

The microbial evidence is also mixed but overall supports a pro-fermentative shift. This is consistent with a fermentable-substrate mechanism in which oligosaccharides are selectively fermented by gut bacteria to produce SCFAs [N5-F3]. The same study also reported increased diversity of intestinal microflora and altered bacterial composition, including beneficial taxa and reduced potentially harmful taxa [N3-F1].

The broader review explains that fermentation of soybean carbohydrates produces short-chain fatty acids that can be used as an energy source by animals, and that dietary supplementation with soybean oligosaccharides increases SCFAs while decreasing protein-derived catabolites in the intestinal luminal content [N4-R4][N3-F1]. This supports the view that oligosaccharides can alter microbial fermentation patterns in a direction that may benefit host metabolism and intestinal homeostasis.

On shifts in dominant bacterial taxa and community structure, the evidence points to changes in community composition rather than a single fixed “prebiotic” signature. The GOS study in piglets found that microbial communities clustered distinctly pre- versus post-weaning, and that post-weaning GOS effects were more detectable [N1-F2]. The SBOS study in weaned piglets found increased diversity and changes in the relative abundance of beneficial versus pathogen-like taxa [N3-F1]. These findings indicate that oligosaccharide supplementation can shift community structure, but the direction and magnitude depend on the oligosaccharide type, dose, and timing [N1-F2][N3-F1].

Overall, the integrated evidence suggests that soy oligosaccharides can have beneficial effects on intestinal physiology and microbial activity in weaning piglets, including improved intestinal barrier markers, altered bacterial composition, and increased SCFA production.
